sections.h2: Can a squatter take title to a Virginia house?
sections.html:
Only after a long period, and the statute sets a time limit rather than a simple recipe. Virginia law bars anyone from entering or suing to recover land unless it is done within fifteen years after the right first accrued to that person or to someone through whom he claims (Va. Code 8.01-236). That limitation is the rule underneath adverse possession: once an owner's right to recover has expired, a person in long possession can argue the owner is out of time.

The statutes we read do not list the elements a court weighs, so the details of a claim, such as what kind of possession counts, come from court decisions. A Virginia attorney can tell you how those decisions apply to a particular property.

The clock also has a ceiling for owners with a legal disability. No disability, and no adding together of disabilities, preserves a right to enter or sue for more than twenty-five years after it first accrued, even if the person was disabled the entire time (Va. Code 8.01-237).

sections.h2: Why does a vacant or inherited house raise the issue?
sections.html:
A house that nobody checks on is the easiest place for an unwelcome occupant to settle in. Heirs who live out of state, owners in a nursing home, and estates waiting for probate all leave properties empty for months. Virginia has 95 counties and 38 independent cities, with Fairfax County the largest jurisdiction and more than one-third of residents in Northern Virginia, so a vacant house can be anywhere from a dense suburb to a rural mountain parcel (Wikipedia, Virginia).

Practical steps that cost little:

  • Post clear no trespassing signs and tell the occupant in writing to leave.
  • Keep dated photos and records of who has keys, utilities and mail.
  • Pay property tax on time so the property does not also face a delinquency suit.
  • Visit on a schedule, or ask a neighbor or property manager to do so.

sections.h2: What can an owner do about an unlawful occupant?
sections.html:
The statutes give an owner two court routes. The first is a motion for judgment in circuit court when someone makes a forcible or unlawful entry on land, or a tenant keeps possession after the right has expired (Va. Code 8.01-124). The action must be brought within three years after the entry or detainer.

The second is a summons for unlawful detainer. The owner presents a sworn statement of the facts to a magistrate, or to a clerk or judge of a general district court, who issues the summons. It must be served at least 10 days before the return day (Va. Code 8.01-126).

The statute also has a faster track for single-family homes. If the owner of a residential single family dwelling files, and the court finds all three of the following, an emergency hearing is held as soon as practicable and within 14 days of filing, or at the latest within 30 days:

  • no rental agreement exists or ever existed between the owner and the occupant;
  • the occupant lives there without the owner's permission;
  • the owner gave the occupant written notice to vacate at least 72 hours before filing.

The text of this section has more than one version with different effective dates, so confirm the current wording with the court clerk before you file.

sections.h2: What does the court case look like step by step?
sections.html:
The table summarizes what the statutes say about the main stages of an unlawful detainer.

StageWhat the statute provides
NoticeWritten notice to vacate at least 72 hours before filing, for the emergency single family hearing
SummonsIssued on the owner's sworn statement; served at least 10 days before the return day
HearingEmergency hearing within 14 days of filing when the conditions are met, otherwise within 30 days at the latest
JudgmentJudgment for the premises, plus proven damages and rent owed; possession can be ordered at the first hearing
AppealWithin 10 days, with bond posted and writ tax paid within 10 days
EvictionSheriff serves notice at least 72 hours before executing the writ, and not before the 10-day appeal period ends

At the initial hearing the plaintiff can receive a final, appealable judgment for possession and an order of possession. On request, the court can split the case and set a later date, no more than 120 days out, to fix final rent and damages (Va. Code 8.01-128). If the owner wins, the judge can order the writ of eviction to issue immediately on request. An indigent defendant does not need to post an appeal bond (Va. Code 8.01-129).

sections.h2: Is staying on the property after being told to leave a crime?
sections.html:
It can be. A person who goes onto or stays on another's land, buildings or premises after being forbidden to do so, orally, in writing or by a posted sign, is guilty of a Class 1 misdemeanor (Va. Code 18.2-119). The statute applies to the owner, lessee, custodian or their agent who gave the warning.

A criminal charge is separate from the civil case that decides possession. The court process above is how possession is decided.

sections.h2: What if the occupant is a former owner after a foreclosure?
sections.html: A former owner still in a single-family home on the day of a foreclosure sale becomes a tenant at sufferance. The successor owner can end that tenancy with a written termination notice given at least three days before the termination date, then file an unlawful detainer. The former owner owes fair market rent from the date of the foreclosure until leaving, plus damages, reasonable attorney fees and court costs (Va. Code 8.01-126).

sections.h2: How does an occupant problem affect selling the house?
sections.html:
It affects price, timing and who will buy. A buyer who needs a loan will generally need the home empty and inspectable, and an open court case can delay that. A cash buyer who purchases as-is can sometimes take the property with the occupant issue still pending, so ask the buyer whether they will do that and who handles the legal filing.

Keep in mind that the seller remains responsible for taxes until closing. If the house is behind on tax, the lien ranks ahead of other liens, and a long delinquency can lead to a judicial sale, so a tax payoff may be part of the same closing.

Before choosing a path, write down every fact about how the person got in: any lease, any text or email permission, the dates and what you have done to demand that they leave. A short consultation with a Virginia attorney can tell you whether to file for unlawful detainer first or negotiate a move-out date.

faqs.q: How many years does adverse possession take in Virginia?
faqs.a: The statute cited for the underlying limitation is fifteen years from when an owner's right to enter or sue first accrued. Court decisions decide what a claimant must prove, so talk to a Virginia attorney about specific facts.

faqs.q: Can I change the locks and remove a squatter myself?
faqs.a: Do not rely on that. The statutes give owners court routes, a motion for judgment in circuit court or a summons for unlawful detainer, and an eviction is carried out by the sheriff under a writ. Ask an attorney before taking any step yourself.

faqs.q: How fast can an unlawful detainer be heard?
faqs.a: For a single-family home with no rental agreement, no permission and a 72 hour written notice, an emergency hearing is set within 14 days of filing, or at the latest within 30 days.

An appeal to circuit court must be taken within 10 days, with bond and the writ tax paid within that time, and the sheriff cannot evict before the 10-day period ends. Indigent defendants are not required to post a bond.

faqs.q: Is trespass a crime in Virginia?
faqs.a: Staying after being forbidden to remain, orally, in writing or by posted sign, is a Class 1 misdemeanor under Va. Code 18.2-119.

faqs.q: Can I sell a house that has an unwelcome occupant?
faqs.a: Yes, but expect the occupant to affect buyers and timing. As-is buyers may accept that risk, and your closing agent will need a clear plan for possession.
